vignette: He sits on the edge of the chair, shoulders drawn tight toward his ears. When the radiator clicks in the hallway, his head snaps toward the sound before he catches himself and exhales. He is twenty-two now, enrolled in his final year of urban planning, but the posture he carries belongs to a different landscape. Two years ago, he travels to a coastal province fractured by artillery. At nineteen, he volunteers with a mobile relief clinic, trading textbooks for triage manuals. The memories do not arrive as stories; they arrive as weather. He describes the afternoon the western ridge collapses, when the sky turns bruised iron and the ground stops breathing. He remembers wet plaster and copper, the tarp shuddering under debris, and the desperate pressure of a boy's fingers around his wrist as the ceiling groans. He digs until his knuckles split. He brings the boy home, but the boy's mother does not survive. He returns to campus in the spring, convinced he can simply turn the page. He attends lectures on zoning laws, surrounded by peers debating studio critiques. For weeks, he moves through the routine like a ghost. Then the intrusions begin. A firecracker at a neighborhood festival sends him under his desk, palms slick, breath short. The smell of diesel from a basement generator triggers nausea. He starts avoiding the library after 4 p.m., claiming it is too crowded, when the shadows stretching across the reading tables feel like corridors he has learned to navigate in a hurry. His apartment becomes a series of precautions. He checks the deadbolt six times before sleep. He sleeps with his back to the wall, a heavy flashlight within arm's reach. Sleep fractures. He wakes standing in his kitchen, convinced he hears boots on gravel, only to find his hands shaking so badly he cannot pour water. During a group project last month, his professor asks him to present his site analysis. When the clicker advances the slide, the sound fractures into gunfire in his head. He stands frozen until his partner touches his elbow. "You okay?" he asks. He nods, smiles, and goes to the restroom to splash cold water on his face until the room stops tilting. He stops calling old friends. The distance between their concerns and the memory of a torn tourniquet feels insurmountable. Some days he feels like a building left open to the rain, all his supports washed out but the frame still standing. Other days, the numbness is so complete he watches his own hands arrange books on his desk and wonders whose they are. His mother still calls from the province, her voice crackling through the connection, asking when he will come home for the festival. He changes the subject. In this moment, he watches dust motes drift in the afternoon light. His fingers trace the seam of his jeans, once, twice, three times. He does not look at the clock. When I ask him how the week has been, he shifts his weight, rolls his shoulders back, and meets my eyes. "I got through the studio review," he says, voice quiet. "But I haven't slept since Tuesday." He pauses, listening to the distant hum of the city beyond the window, and waits for the next question to land.
